title: Tier 2 capstone: end-to-end incident handling
summary: Work one realistic account-compromise incident from first report to post-incident notes, pulling together everything you learned across the course. You will rule out an outage, investigate sign-ins, contain the account, clean up attacker persistence, and document the root cause.
objectives: Triage a user report and rule out a service outage before assuming compromise
Investigate suspicious sign-ins in Microsoft Entra ID and confirm scope
Contain a compromised account by resetting credentials and revoking active sessions
Find and remove attacker persistence such as inbox rules and mail forwarding
Use message trace, quarantine, and Defender to assess spread and remediate
Communicate, escalate, and write clear root-cause and post-incident notes in the ticket

quiz.q: A user reports they cannot send email and that colleagues received strange messages from their address. What should you check FIRST before assuming the account is compromised?
options: Microsoft 365 Service health to rule out a wider outage
Buy the user a new laptop
Reinstall Outlook on every device in the office
quiz.why: Service health tells you whether the symptoms come from a known Microsoft outage. Confirming scope first stops you from chasing a compromise that is really a platform incident — and vice versa.

quiz.q: In Microsoft Entra ID, which signal most strongly suggests an account was compromised rather than the user simply travelling?
options: A single successful sign-in from the user's usual city
Successful sign-ins from an unfamiliar country plus impossible-travel and legacy-auth attempts
The user changing their display name
A failed sign-in once on Monday morning
quiz.why: Impossible travel, an unfamiliar location, and legacy or basic-auth sign-ins together are classic compromise indicators. One normal sign-in or a single typo'd password is not.

quiz.q: After confirming compromise, what is the correct CONTAINMENT order for the account?
options: Tell the user to ignore it and monitor for a week
Revoke sessions only and leave the old password active
Reset the password, then revoke active sessions, then re-confirm MFA
Delete the account permanently with no investigation
quiz.why: Resetting the password stops new sign-ins with the stolen credential, revoking sessions kills tokens the attacker already holds, and re-confirming MFA restores trusted access. Skipping the revoke leaves live tokens working.

quiz.q: Why must you check the mailbox for inbox rules and mail forwarding after a compromise?
options: Forwarding is required for MFA to work
Inbox rules store the user's password
Attackers plant rules to hide replies or auto-forward mail, giving them persistence after the password change
quiz.why: A planted rule that deletes or forwards security mail lets the attacker keep reading messages and hide their tracks even after you reset the password. Removing persistence is part of remediation, not optional.

quiz.q: Name the Exchange Online tool you would use to see whether messages were actually sent from the mailbox and where they were delivered.
quiz.answer: Message trace (Get-MessageTrace in PowerShell, or the message trace report in the Exchange admin center / Defender portal).
quiz.why: Message trace shows the path and status of individual messages, so you can confirm what the attacker sent, to whom, and whether it was delivered or blocked.

quiz.q: In one or two sentences, what belongs in your post-incident / root-cause note once the account is secured?
quiz.answer: A short timeline of what happened, the likely root cause (e.g. phishing link harvested the credential), the actions you took to contain and remediate, and any follow-ups such as user security awareness or tightening conditional access.
quiz.why: Good post-incident notes let the next tech understand the incident at a glance, support escalation or audit, and feed prevention so the same compromise does not recur.

body_markdown:
## The ticket lands

A user, Priya, raises a ticket: she **can't send email**, and two colleagues have asked her why she emailed them a strange "shared invoice" link. This is your capstone. Everything you learned this course — hardware and OS basics, networking, identity, email, security, and Microsoft 365 admin — comes together in one incident. You will work it end to end like a real **Tier 2** tech.

Don't jump to a fix. Start with **triage**: when did it start, what exactly does "can't send" look like (a bounce? a block?), and has anything changed. Log it in the ticket as you go.

## Rule out an outage first

Before you assume compromise, confirm scope. Open the Microsoft 365 admin center and check **Service health**.

```text
Microsoft 365 admin center > Health > Service health > Exchange Online
```

If there's an active advisory affecting send/receive, this may be a platform incident, not Priya. No advisory, and only Priya is affected with odd outbound mail? That points at an **account compromise** — likely the aftermath of a phishing link that harvested her password.

## Investigate the sign-ins

Go to **Microsoft Entra ID** and review Priya's sign-in logs. You're looking for **impossible travel**, sign-ins from an unfamiliar country, and **legacy authentication** attempts.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "AuditLog.Read.All","User.ReadWrite.All"
Get-MgAuditLogSignIn -Filter "userPrincipalName eq 'priya@contoso.com'" -Top 25 |
  Select-Object createdDateTime, ipAddress, @{n='City';e={$_.Location.City}}, status
```

A successful sign-in from another continent minutes after a normal one confirms it. Note the timeline in the ticket.

## Contain the account

Now stop the bleeding, in order. **Reset the password**, then **revoke active sessions** so any tokens the attacker already holds stop working, then re-confirm **MFA**.

```powershell
# Disable sign-in while you work, then revoke live tokens
Update-MgUser -UserId priya@contoso.com -AccountEnabled:$false
Revoke-MgUserSignInSession -UserId priya@contoso.com
```

Reset the password in the admin center, re-enable the account, and confirm MFA is registered. The stolen credential is now useless.

## Remove persistence and assess spread

A password reset alone is not enough. Attackers plant **inbox rules** and **mail forwarding** to keep reading mail and hide replies. Connect to Exchange Online and check.

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline
Get-InboxRule -Mailbox priya@contoso.com | Format-List Name, Description, ForwardTo, DeleteMessage
Get-Mailbox priya@contoso.com | Format-List ForwardingSmtpAddress
```

Delete any rule you didn't expect. Then run a **message trace** to see what actually went out and to whom, and check **quarantine** and **Microsoft Defender for Office 365** for the phishing message and its blast radius.

```powershell
Get-MessageTrace -SenderAddress priya@contoso.com -StartDate (Get-Date).AddDays(-2) -EndDate (Get-Date)
```

## Communicate, escalate, document

Tell Priya what happened in plain language and that her account is secure. Warn the colleagues who received the link **not to click it**. If the spread is wide or other accounts look affected, **escalate** to Tier 3 / security. Finally, write the **root-cause and post-incident note** in the ticket: timeline, likely cause (phishing), actions taken, and follow-ups such as security-awareness training and tighter conditional access.

## Your task

Write the full incident up as a single ticket: triage notes, the outage check, the sign-in evidence, your containment steps, the persistence you removed, the message-trace findings, and a three-line root-cause note. Treat it as the write-up you'd hand to a hiring manager.

slides.narration: Time to stop the bleeding, and order matters here. First reset the password, which makes the stolen credential useless. Then revoke active sessions, because the attacker may already be holding live tokens that keep working even after a password change. Revoking sign-in sessions kills those tokens. Then re-confirm M F A so trusted access is restored. A common mistake is resetting the password but forgetting to revoke sessions, which leaves the attacker logged in.

slides.title: Remove attacker persistence
bullets: A password reset alone is not enough.
Attackers plant inbox rules and mail forwarding.
Check Get-InboxRule and ForwardingSmtpAddress.
Delete anything you didn't expect.
slides.code:
Connect-ExchangeOnline
Get-InboxRule -Mailbox priya@contoso.com | Format-List Name, ForwardTo, DeleteMessage
Get-Mailbox priya@contoso.com | Format-List ForwardingSmtpAddress
slides.narration: Here's the step people forget. A password reset on its own is not enough. Attackers plant inbox rules and mail forwarding so they can keep reading mail and hide their replies, even after you've changed the password. So connect to Exchange Online, list the inbox rules with Get dash Inbox Rule, and check the mailbox forwarding address. If you find a rule or a forward you didn't expect, delete it. That's how you remove their persistence.

slides.title: Assess the spread
bullets: Run a message trace to see what actually went out.
Check who received the phishing message.
Review quarantine and Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
Understand the blast radius before you close out.
slides.narration: Now assess how far it spread. Run a message trace with Get dash Message Trace to see exactly what was sent from Priya's mailbox over the last couple of days and where it was delivered. Then check quarantine and Microsoft Defender for Office three sixty five to find the phishing message and understand its blast radius. You need to know who actually received the bad link before you can say the incident is contained.

Warn colleagues not to click the link.
Escalate to Tier 3 or security if spread is wide.
Keep the ticket updated throughout.

State the likely root cause, e.g. phishing.
List the actions you took to contain and remediate.
Add follow-ups: awareness training, conditional access.

Include a timeline of what happened, the likely root cause such as a phishing link that harvested the password, the actions you took to contain and remediate, and any follow-ups, like security awareness training for the user or tightening conditional access policies. This note is what lets the next tech, or a hiring manager, understand the whole incident at a glance.

bullets: Triage, rule out outage, investigate sign-ins.

Task: write the whole incident up as one ticket.
slides.narration: Let's recap the capstone. You triaged the report and ruled out an outage with Service health. You investigated the sign-ins in Entra. You contained the account by resetting the password, revoking sessions, and confirming M F A. You removed the attacker's inbox rules and forwarding, ran a message trace, and checked Defender. Then you communicated, escalated, and documented the root cause. Your task: write this entire incident up as a single ticket, with triage notes, your outage check, the sign-in evidence, your containment steps, the persistence you removed, the message-trace findings, and a three-line root-cause note. Treat it as the write-up you'd proudly hand to a hiring manager. That's your whole course, brought together. Well done.
